tips.title: Problème is masculine
tips.body: Despite the final -e, **le problème** is masculine: *le plus grand problème*, *un problème grave*. So is **l'environnement**. Both appear in almost every answer on this topic, so getting them wrong is very visible.

tips.title: Noun or clause decides the connector
tips.body: **À cause de** and **grâce à** take a **noun**. **Parce que** and **car** take a **clause with a verb**. Decide which you have before choosing: *parce que la circulation* is wrong because there is no verb.

tips.title: Quantity takes de with no article
tips.body: *Trop de*, *assez de*, *beaucoup de*, *moins de*, *peu de* — all followed by **de** alone, whatever the gender: *trop de voitures*, never *trop des voitures*. The one exception is **la plupart des**.

tips.title: Si on ne fait rien, … sera
tips.body: **Si + present, + future** is the cheapest complex sentence available: *Si on ne fait rien, la situation **sera** pire.* It is easy to build, unmistakably complex, and fits the end of any answer about a problem.

steps.title: Les problèmes
steps.body:
The vocabulary here is mostly nouns, and the marks are mostly in their **genders**. Learn each one with its article, because you will need it for the adjective as well.

The problems that come up most often:

- **la pollution** — pollution
- **le réchauffement climatique** — global warming
- **les déchets** — rubbish, waste (always plural)
- **la circulation** — traffic, and **les embouteillages** — traffic jams
- **la sécheresse** — drought, and **les inondations** — floods
- **la déforestation** — deforestation
- **le gaspillage** — waste, in the sense of wastefulness

Two traps. *La circulation* means **traffic**, not circulation in the medical sense. And *les déchets* is the rubbish itself, while *le gaspillage* is the **wasting** of something — food, water, energy. A question about *le gaspillage alimentaire* is about food waste as a behaviour, not about bins.

steps.title: Dire que c'est un problème
steps.body:
Naming a problem is worth one mark. Saying **why it matters** is worth the rest.

Three patterns carry most answers:

- **Le plus grand problème, c'est …** — The biggest problem is …
- **Ce qui m'inquiète le plus, c'est …** — What worries me most is …
- **À mon avis, … est un problème grave** — In my opinion, … is a serious problem

Then give a cause with **à cause de** or a consequence with **donc** or **ce qui**:

> *Le plus grand problème, c'est la pollution de l'air, **à cause de** la circulation.*
> *Il y a trop de déchets dans les rues, **ce qui est** vraiment moche.*

Note the difference between **à cause de** and **grâce à**. Both mean *because of*, but **à cause de** is for something **bad** and **grâce à** for something **good**. *Grâce à la pollution* would be a serious error.

steps.title: Trop de, assez de, moins de
steps.body:
Quantity words are how you turn a noun into a complaint, and they all behave the same way: **quantity + de**, with **no article**.

- **trop de** — too much, too many
- **beaucoup de** — a lot of
- **assez de** — enough
- **peu de** — few, little
- **moins de** — less, fewer
- **plus de** — more

> *Il y a **trop de** voitures.* — There are too many cars.
> *Il n'y a pas **assez de** poubelles.* — There aren't enough bins.

Never *trop des voitures*. The *de* swallows the article, whatever the gender or number.

One exception worth knowing: **la plupart** takes **des**. *La plupart **des** gens* — most people.

Il y a beaucoup de déchets.
Il n'y a pas assez de poubelles.

steps.title: Les causes et les conséquences
steps.body:
A top answer links a problem to a cause **and** a consequence. The connectors are short and worth memorising as a set.

**Causes**

- *à cause de* — because of
- *parce que* — because (followed by a clause)
- *car* — because, slightly more formal, joins two clauses

**Consequences**

- *donc* — so, therefore
- *ce qui* — which (referring to the whole idea before it)
- *par conséquent* — consequently
- *cela entraîne* — this leads to

Put together:

> *Il y a trop de voitures **parce que** les transports en commun sont chers, **donc** l'air est pollué, **ce qui** est mauvais pour la santé.*

One sentence, one problem, a cause and two consequences. That structure is the whole skill.

Be careful with **parce que** and **à cause de**. *Parce que* is followed by a **clause** with a verb; *à cause de* is followed by a **noun**. *Parce que la circulation* is wrong — it needs a verb.

steps.title: Construire une réponse complète
steps.body: A typical speaking or writing question is *Quel est le plus grand problème de l'environnement dans ta région ?* Here is how to build four marks' worth rather than one.

visuals.problem: Quel est le plus grand problème dans ta région ?

steps.text: **Name it**: *À mon avis, le plus grand problème, c'est la circulation.*
steps.note: one mark, and the frame is reusable

steps.text: **Give a cause**: *…, parce que tout le monde va au travail en voiture.*
**Give a consequence**: *…, donc l'air est pollué et il y a beaucoup d'embouteillages.*
**React to it**: *Ce qui m'inquiète le plus, c'est l'effet sur la santé des enfants.*
**Add a tense**: *Avant, il y **avait** moins de voitures ici.*
Five sentences, one topic, four structures, three tenses

steps.title: À toi : les problèmes chez toi
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Traduis en français.

1. There is too much traffic.
2. The river is polluted because of the factory.
3. There aren't enough bins in the park.

**Partie B.** Réponds en français, en phrases complètes.

4. Quel est le plus grand problème de l'environnement dans ta région ? Donne une cause.
5. Quelle en est la conséquence ?
6. Qu'est-ce qui t'inquiète le plus ? Pourquoi ?

**Partie C.** Écris cinq phrases répondant à *Quel est le plus grand problème dans ta région ?*, en suivant les cinq étapes de l'étape 5. Utilise au moins deux temps.

Before you write, decide whether each connector needs a **noun** or a **clause**.

steps.title: Aller plus loin: nuancer
steps.body:
At the top band, an answer stops sounding like a list of complaints and starts sounding like a view. Three moves do that.

**1. Concede something.** *Bien sûr*, *c'est vrai que*, *par contre*, *cependant*.

> *C'est vrai que la ville a construit des pistes cyclables, **mais** il y a toujours trop de voitures.*

A sentence that admits the other side is far stronger than one that does not, and it shows a conjunction you would otherwise never use.

**2. Rank the problems.** *Le plus grave*, *moins important*, *le pire*.

> *La pollution de l'air est **plus grave que** les déchets, **car** elle touche tout le monde.*

Ranking forces a comparative and a reason into the same sentence.

**3. Look forward.** *Si on ne fait rien*, *il faudra*, *dans dix ans*.

> ***Si on ne fait rien**, la situation **sera** pire dans dix ans.*

That is the *si* + present + future pattern, and it is one of the highest-value structures available to you: it is easy to build and it is unmistakably a complex sentence.

**One accuracy warning.** *Problème* is **masculine** despite the *-e*: *un problème grave*, *le plus grand problème*. Writing *une problème* is a visible error in a sentence you are otherwise being rewarded for.

And **l'environnement** is masculine, with the article elided: *l'environnement est menacé*.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- Learn each problem **with its article**: **la** pollution, **le** réchauffement climatique, **les** déchets, **la** circulation, **le** gaspillage.
- **Problème** is **masculine** despite the -e. **L'environnement** is masculine too.
- *La circulation* is **traffic**; *les déchets* is rubbish; *le gaspillage* is **wastefulness**.
- Quantity words take **de** with **no article**: *trop de*, *assez de*, *beaucoup de*, *moins de*. Never *trop des*.
- **La plupart** is the exception: *la plupart **des** gens*.
- **À cause de** takes a **noun** and is for something bad; **grâce à** is for something good.
- **Parce que** and **car** take a **clause** with a verb.
- Consequences: **donc**, **ce qui**, **par conséquent**, **cela entraîne**.
- A full answer: name the problem, give a cause, give a consequence, react, and use another tense.
- To nuance: **c'est vrai que … mais**, **plus grave que … car**, and **si on ne fait rien, … sera**.
- **Si + present + future** is the highest-value structure here.
- Depth beats breadth: one problem developed beats five problems listed.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Modèle.**

> *À mon avis, **le plus grand problème** dans ma région, **c'est la circulation**. Il y a beaucoup **trop de voitures** le matin, **parce que** presque tout le monde va au travail en voiture. **Par conséquent**, l'air est pollué et il y a des embouteillages partout, **ce qui est** vraiment pénible. **Ce qui m'inquiète le plus, c'est** l'effet sur la santé des enfants, **car** ils marchent au bord de la route tous les jours. **Avant, il y avait** moins de voitures ici, et **si on ne fait rien, la situation sera** encore pire dans dix ans.*

**What earns the marks.** *Le plus grand* agrees with the **masculine** *problème*. *Trop de* with no article. *Parce que* with a clause. Three tenses: present, **imperfect** (*il y avait*), **future** (*sera*). And the *si + present + future* pattern in the last sentence.

questions.prompt: Traduis en anglais naturel : « Dans ma ville, il y a trop de circulation à cause des transports en commun qui coûtent cher. Par conséquent, l'air est pollué, ce qui est mauvais pour la santé. Si on ne fait rien, la situation sera pire. »
questions.solution: In my town there is too much traffic because public transport is expensive. As a result, the air is polluted, which is bad for people's health. If we do nothing, the situation will get worse.

Renders *si on ne fait rien … sera* with the right English tenses

questions.modelAnswer:
**Traduction.**

> In my town **there is too much traffic because public transport is expensive**. **As a result**, the air is polluted, **which is bad for people's health**. **If we do nothing, the situation will get worse.**

**Three things to notice.**

- *À cause des transports en commun **qui coûtent cher*** is a relative clause; English turns it into a simple *because public transport is expensive*.
- ***Ce qui*** refers back to the **whole idea**, so it becomes *which*, not *what*.
- ***Si on ne fait rien … sera*** is *si* + present + future. English matches it: **if we do nothing, … will**. Note *on* becomes **we**, not *one*.

examTechnique.body:
Pick **one** problem and develop it. Naming five problems scores less than one problem with a cause, a consequence and an opinion.

Build the answer in the same five moves every time: name it, cause, consequence, react, and add a tense other than the present. The frames are reusable, so practise them once and they work for any topic.

Check each connector against what follows it. A noun needs *à cause de*; a verb needs *parce que* or *car*.

After a quantity word, write *de* and nothing else.

Finish with *si on ne fait rien, … sera*. It is a complex structure you can build reliably under pressure, and it shows the future tense as well.

Check the genders of *problème* and *environnement* before you hand the paper in.
examinerErrors: Writing *une problème*. It is masculine despite the -e.
Writing *trop des voitures* instead of *trop de voitures*.
Using *grâce à* for something bad, which reverses the meaning.
Following *parce que* with a noun instead of a clause.
Listing several problems instead of developing one.
Writing the whole answer in the present tense.
Confusing *les déchets*, the rubbish, with *le gaspillage*, the wasting.
Using *si* with the future in the first half: it is *si + present*, then the future.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer commits to one problem and keeps the whole response about it, so each sentence develops the last rather than starting again. It links cause to consequence explicitly, choosing the connector to fit what follows it. It concedes something before disagreeing, which shows a conjunction and a balanced view at once. It moves through at least three tenses without strain, usually by saying what things used to be like and what will happen if nothing changes, and it ends on *si on ne fait rien*, which is the clearest signal of control available in this topic.
